title: Vera Rubin: The Whirling Galaxies and Dark Matter
source_book: Rotation of the Andromeda Nebula from a Spectroscopic Survey of Emission Regions
source_author: Vera C. Rubin & W. Kent Ford Jr.
authenticity_note: Directly based on Vera Rubin and Kent Ford's 1970 breakthrough measurements of flat galactic rotation curves in Andromeda and other spiral galaxies, providing the definitive observational evidence for Dark Matter.
summary: Observing spiral galaxies with an advanced spectrograph, Vera Rubin found that stars at the outer edges of galaxies whirled just as fast as stars near the center, defying Newtonian gravity. Her flat rotation curves proved that galaxies are embedded in massive, invisible halos of 'Dark Matter' that make up most of the universe's mass.
content:
According to Sir Isaac Newton's laws of universal gravitation, planets close to the Sun, like Mercury, zip around their orbits at high speeds, while distant planets like Neptune crawl slowly because gravity weakens with distance ($F \propto 1/r^2$). For centuries, astronomers assumed the same law applied to spiral galaxies: stars at the bright galactic core should rotate fast, while stars far out on the shadowy spiral arms should drift sluggishly.

In the late 1960s, American astronomer Vera Rubin, working at the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism in Washington, D.C., decided to test this fundamental assumption. Partnering with instrument builder Kent Ford, Rubin traveled to Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona with an ultra-sensitive electronic spectrograph.

Rubin aimed their telescope at the glowing hydrogen clouds of the Andromeda galaxy and dozens of other spiral galaxies. By measuring the Doppler shift of light from stars across the galactic disks, she carefully plotted their orbital velocity against distance from the core—a plot called a galactic rotation curve.

She expected the curve to plunge downward at the outer edges. Instead, Rubin was stunned: the curves were completely flat! Stars at the furthest fringes were hurtling through space at hundreds of kilometers per second—just as fast as the inner stars!

By all laws of classical physics, these runaway outer stars should have flown apart, tearing the galaxies to shreds. The visible matter—all the blazing stars, gas, and dust combined—provided less than ten percent of the gravity needed to hold the galaxies together!

Rubin realized that galaxies were not just what our eyes can see. Every galaxy was anchored inside a gargantuan, invisible halo of mysterious, non-luminous mass: **Dark Matter**.

Vera Rubin's precise observational data forced astrophysicists to confront a humbling truth: the familiar baryonic matter of stars, planets, and human beings constitutes barely five percent of the cosmos. Over eighty-five percent of the matter in the universe is dark and completely unknown.

stem_vocabulary.definition: A plot of the orbital speeds of visible stars or gas in a galaxy versus their radial distance from the galactic center.
Hypothetical matter that does not emit or interact with electromagnetic radiation, making it invisible, but exerts gravitational pull.
The constant orbital velocity observed at large distances from a galactic center, indicating unaccounted mass.
A massive, roughly spherical region of dark matter enveloping a spiral galaxy.
